chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who has a female servant, and he says: 'She is for so-and-so to serve him as long as he lives, and when he dies, she is free.' The servant escapes before the man dies by five or six years, then his heirs find her. Is it for them to employ her after she has escaped? He said: 'No, when the man dies, she has become free.'

Because the meaning in this report is that the manumission (tadbir) was suspended upon the death of the man for whom she was designated to serve. Where she escaped, it prevented the man (while alive) from exercising authority over her, and that does not invalidate the manumission. The first case was that the manumission was suspended upon the death of the master; where she escaped, her escaping prevented her master from exercising authority over her, and that invalidated the manumission. There is no contradiction between the two reports, and the first report adds clarification to what was narrated.

key_terms.التَّدْبِير: Conditional manumission of a slave upon the master's death

ai.seo_question: Does a slave's escape before the master's death invalidate conditional manumission (tadbir)?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling to resolve the apparent contradiction between narrations regarding 'tadbir' (conditional manumission) by distinguishing between the master's direct authority and the designated heir's contingent right. The scholar explains that since the escape suspends rather than nullifies the master's power, the condition for freedom remains intact upon his death. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on preserving the integrity of the master's intent in manumission contracts.
